in_text_mentions: t relevant medical history, presented to the emergency department after sustaining a viper bite at home. On arrival, she complained of nausea and vomiting and was markedly hypotensive, with a blood pressure of 52/34 mmHg. Physical examination identified a single puncture mark on the right index finger, surrounded by a hemorrhagic blister and diffuse swelling of the hand (Figure 1). Initial management included fluid resuscitation, local wound care, and close monitoring. During the first hour of observation, the patient developed progressive edema involving the right hand and forearm (Figure 2).

in_text_mentions: On physical examination, swelling on her right hand with a fang mark, sweating, bradycardic, bradypnea, and salivation were observed. Vital signs included heart rate 30 bpm and were essentially nearing full cardiac arrest with unrecordable other vital signs. Immediately Pediatric Advanced Life Support (PALS) was started. After completion of three rounds of PALS, the carotid pulse was palpable and the patient reverted to spontaneous circulation (ROSC). The patient was moved to the pediatric intensive care unit (PICU) for further management (Figure 1).

panels.rationale: Single clinical photograph of a human hand showing severe cytotoxic snake-venom tissue damage on the dorsal hand, consistent with the article title 'Snake bite - cytotoxic effects of snake venom: a rare clinical image' and the caption 'damaged tissue on the dorsal hand'. Real patient image, no third-party copyright, no competing disease. The visible necrotic, denuded, hemorrhagic tissue supports bite-site necrosis with peribite ecchymosis. [raw subtype: cytotoxic]
